The simulated teaching cohorts

Source: vignettes/simulated-data.Rmd
simulated-data.Rmd

Every dataset in WeGrowHealthR comes from one generator, wgh_simulate(). Real growth records of children cannot be shared, so the package ships simulated cohorts instead. The wgh_like preset is set so that a cohort resembles the published results of the school health cohort studied in the research program (see wgh_references()): the same patterns, the same directions of effect and numbers of a similar size. It does not reproduce published values, and nothing computed from it is a finding.

This vignette explains how the generator works, how to check the resemblance, how to change the simulated world, and how to use the truth file to test methods.

Simulating a cohort 

library(WeGrowHealthR)
sim <- wgh_simulate(20000, seed = 2026)
sim
#> <wgh_sim> preset "wgh_like", seed 2026
#> 42348 visits from 16118 children (19773 enrolled)
#> Mean-curve APHV: boys 12.2 y, girls 9.2 y. PHV: 9.3 and 7 cm/y
#> Simulated data. Results resemble but do not reproduce published findings.

The main arguments are:

  • n_children, the number of children generated before enrolment rules (fewer appear in the visit data, because not every child attends),
  • preset, "wgh_like" (default) or "reference" (a cohort with simple, textbook settings), or a settings list from wgh_preset(),
  • seed, so the same call always gives the same cohort,
  • informative_visits, whether attendance depends on the child’s BMI as in real school data (FALSE makes visits missing at random),
  • style, the column names: "book1" (pid, yearvisit, baz) or "book2" (pid, schoolyear, bmiz),
  • ..., single settings that override the preset, for example years = 2012:2025.

The result is a list:

names(sim)
#> [1] "visits"      "roster"      "truth_child" "truth_visit" "pop_peaks"  
#> [6] "settings"    "call"
head(sim$visits)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 13
#>   pid     sex    site  dob        yearvisit examdate     age height weight   bmi
#>   <chr>   <fct>  <fct> <date>         <int> <date>     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 C000002 Female Site1 2005-07-08      2019 2019-12-08 14.4    156.   46.2  19.0
#> 2 C000002 Female Site1 2005-07-08      2020 2020-12-30 15.5    158.   45.3  18.1
#> 3 C000002 Female Site1 2005-07-08      2022 2022-09-19 17.2    159.   49.8  19.8
#> 4 C000003 Male   Site3 2010-07-12      2018 2018-11-11  8.33   124.   26.9  17.4
#> 5 C000003 Male   Site3 2010-07-12      2019 2019-11-25  9.37   130    33.8  20  
#> 6 C000003 Male   Site3 2010-07-12      2020 2020-10-29 10.3    136.   37.1  20.2
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: haz <dbl>, waz <dbl>, baz <dbl>
  • visits holds the measurements, one row per visit, with WHO z-scores,
  • roster lists every child and school year, attended or not,
  • truth_child and truth_visit hold the true values behind the measurements (next sections),
  • pop_peaks the population APHV and PHV implied by the settings,
  • settings the full settings used.

How the children grow

Each child’s height follows a Preece-Baines mean curve for the child’s sex, joined below 6 years to a WHO-shaped early childhood curve. The child’s own curve is the mean curve shifted in size, timing and intensity, as in a SITAR model. Children belong to growth phenotypes (for example early and intense, or late and gentle) that shift these parameters. Adiposity is a stable child trait with a slow drift. It raises BMI, makes puberty slightly earlier and is linked with height. BMI is converted to weight through the WHO reference. Measurement error is added to height and weight. Attendance depends on age, calendar year (with a year of school closures) and, when informative_visits = TRUE, on BMI.

How close is the resemblance?

wgh_targets lists published patterns with acceptable bands, for example the prevalence of overweight and obesity by sex, the APHV of boys and girls and the spread of individual timing. wgh_resemblance_report() computes each pattern in a simulated cohort and checks it against its band.

head(wgh_targets)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   target                          sex   published lower upper unit  source tuned
#>   <chr>                           <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr> <chr>  <lgl>
#> 1 Visits at largest site (%)      All        67.6    55    75 %     Ho et… TRUE 
#> 2 Visits at smallest site (%)     All         7.4     4    14 %     Ho et… TRUE 
#> 3 Visits under 5 years (%)        All        22.7    15    30 %     Ho et… TRUE 
#> 4 Visits at ages 5 to 11 (%)      All        48.6    38    58 %     Ho et… TRUE 
#> 5 Visits in first year (%)        All         3.4     1     8 %     Ho et… TRUE 
#> 6 Overweight or obesity, 5 to 18… Male       47.7    42    53 %     Ho et… TRUE
rr <- wgh_resemblance_report(sim)
rr

plot(rr, base_size = 9)

Each row of the plot is one pattern. The green area is the acceptable band, the cross the published value and the dot the simulated value (blue inside the band, orange outside). plot(rr, only_failed = TRUE) shows only the patterns outside their band.

Some patterns were used to set the preset (tuned = TRUE). Others were kept out as independent checks, for example the association between BMI and height in childhood and in late adolescence. Passing those checks shows the generator has the right structure, not only the right averages.

Building another world

Because the true structure is known, you can change one setting and see how an analysis responds. wgh_preset() returns all settings, with units documented in the package source.

s <- wgh_preset("wgh_like")
s$beta_tempo_adiposity
#>   Male Female 
#>  -0.15  -0.12
s$beta_tempo_adiposity <- c(Male = 0, Female = 0)     # adiposity no longer changes timing
alt <- wgh_simulate(5000, preset = s, seed = 1)
cor(alt$truth_child$u_adip, alt$truth_child$b_tempo)
#> [1] -0.08284039
cor(sim$truth_child$u_adip, sim$truth_child$b_tempo)
#> [1] -0.2441347

In the altered world, adiposity and timing are unrelated, while in the default world children with more adiposity have earlier timing (negative b). Running the pubertal spurt analysis on both worlds shows whether a method can tell them apart.

wgh_tune_preset() adjusts a few settings automatically so that a preset meets the prevalence and age-distribution targets, which is how the wgh_like preset was set.

The truth file: testing methods

truth_child holds each child’s true SITAR parameters, phenotype and adiposity, and truth_visit the true height and velocity at each visit.

head(sim$truth_child)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 14
#>   pid     sex    site  dob        birth_year phenotype    u_adip  d_adip  z_size
#>   <chr>   <fct>  <fct> <date>          <int> <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 C000001 Female Site1 2001-04-18       2001 Average    -0.217    0.136   2.13  
#> 2 C000002 Female Site1 2005-07-08       2005 Late-gent… -0.533   -0.269  -0.500 
#> 3 C000003 Male   Site3 2010-07-12       2010 Early-int…  0.00160 -0.0435 -1.10  
#> 4 C000004 Male   Site2 2001-11-28       2001 Early-int…  0.260   -0.179   0.0330
#> 5 C000005 Female Site1 2005-08-11       2005 Average    -1.61    -0.454   0.405 
#> 6 C000006 Male   Site1 2011-04-13       2011 Average     0.209   -0.247  -0.0980
#> # ℹ 5 more variables: a_size <dbl>, b_tempo <dbl>, c_intensity <dbl>,
#> #   aphv_true <dbl>, phv_true <dbl>

wgh_truth_check() compares estimates with the truth, for example the individual APHV from a SITAR model with aphv_true:

boys <- sim$visits[sim$visits$sex == "Male", ]
fit <- wgh_fit_sitar(boys, df = 5, age_range = c(6, 18))
eff <- wgh_sitar_effects(fit)
eff$pid <- eff$id
wgh_truth_check(eff, sim$truth_child, est_col = "aphv", truth_col = "aphv_true")

This is the safest way to learn what a method can and cannot recover.

Bundled datasets

Dataset What it is
growdat A cohort of about 3,300 children from 18 months to 18 years, book 1 column names
growdat_raw growdat as a messy export, for practising cleaning
growdat2_mini A smaller cohort with book 2 column names, with its truth file growdat2_mini_truth
clinical_cases A few dozen children with clinical patterns (wgh_simulate_clinical_cases())
wgh_targets The published patterns used to check resemblance
who_lms, cdc_lms WHO and CDC 2000 LMS reference tables

The full-size cohort used in book 2 can be obtained with wgh_download(). It downloads a frozen copy when a URL is configured, verifying its checksum, and otherwise regenerates the same cohort locally. The result records where it came from in its "provenance" attribute.

small <- wgh_download(url = NULL, n_children = 500)
attr(small, "provenance")[c("source", "n_children", "seed", "preset", "package_version")]
#> $source
#> [1] "regenerated"
#> 
#> $n_children
#> [1] 500
#> 
#> $seed
#> [1] 2026
#> 
#> $preset
#> [1] "wgh_like"
#> 
#> $package_version
#> [1] "1.0.1"
